## In 60 seconds

An AI agent is a loop: a model, usually a large language model (LLM), chooses a tool, reads the
result and chooses again until the goal is met or a step limit is reached
[@yao2023react; @khosravi2026]. That makes agents useful for multi-step EP work, such as literature watch, data
checks, report drafts and simulation runs, and risky in new ways. Errors compound over a chain of
steps, documents can carry hidden instructions, and a confident summary can contain a number that
no tool produced. Published medical agents have been tested on benchmark tasks in a simulated
health record [@jiang2025medagentbench], in simulated consultations [@schmidgall2024agentclinic],
and on rare-disease diagnosis with an expert audit of their reasoning [@zhao2026]. This module
derives how reliability compounds and what a check buys, builds an agent whose guardrails sit
outside the model, attacks it with an injected instruction, and evaluates it on a task suite.

## From the field

- **Benchmarks in a simulated health record (Stanford).** MedAgentBench gives an LLM agent 300
  physician-written tasks over 100 realistic patient records through the standard interfaces of
  electronic health records; the best model completed 69.67% of tasks, with large differences between
  task categories [@jiang2025medagentbench]. A follow-up redesigned the agent's tools so that it no
  longer built raw web requests, which had been prone to syntax errors, and reported 91.0% success
  without memory and 98.0% with a memory of earlier failures [@chen2026medagentbench].
- **Simulated consultations (Stanford and Johns Hopkins).** In AgentClinic, a doctor agent must
  question a patient agent and order tests from a measurement agent within a limited number of
  turns; models did much worse in this sequential format than on the same cases posed as multiple-choice
  questions [@schmidgall2024agentclinic].
- **Traceable reasoning.** DeepRare, a multi-agent system with more than 40 tools for rare-disease
  diagnosis, links each step of its reasoning to evidence. On 163 clinical cases it ranked the right
  diagnosis first for 64.4% of cases, against 54.6% for experienced physicians given the same
  structured input; experts judged 95.4% of its cited references correct, and the errors included
  invented web links [@zhao2026].
- **Tools for numbers.** An LLM agent that called signal-analysis tools estimated heart rate from
  wearable PPG more accurately than LLMs given the data directly, with ECG as the reference
  [@feli2025].
- **Agents that build models.** An LLM-driven loop proposed, validated and selected ECG model designs
  for diastolic dysfunction and was then tested in external cohorts (preprint) [@jamthikar2026].
  Searching many designs against one validation set is the leakage problem of m35 in a new form.
- **EP workflows and devices.** Reviews describe agentic workflows for EP literature, guideline
  monitoring and reports [@patel2025], and an LLM-based system estimated pacemaker battery levels from
  simulated remote-monitoring files for 30 people [@iwai2025].
- **Guardrails as software (NVIDIA).** NeMo Guardrails puts programmable rules between the user and
  the model, independent of the model, for topics, fact-checking and input and output moderation
  [@rebedea2023guardrails].

## Derivations

### What an agent is

| Piece | What it does | EP example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model | Chooses the next action | Decides to check point density before computing velocity |
| Tools | Do the real work, with typed inputs and units | `fill_distance`, `lat_outliers`, `conduction_velocity` |
| State and memory | Keeps what has been done and found | The audit log of a mapping-QC run |
| Control loop | Plan, act, observe, repeat, with a step limit | Up to 20 tool calls per task |
| Policy | Says which actions run, need approval or are refused | Read and compute run; writes need a person |

ReAct made the loop explicit: the model alternates reasoning with actions, such as a search, and
reads each observation before the next step [@yao2023react]. Memory and reflection are central to
Stanford's generative agents, which simulate believable human behaviour [@park2023generative], and
DeepRare's central host keeps a memory bank and revisits its hypotheses in a self-reflection step
[@zhao2026]. The course uses five levels of autonomy, a framework of its own, not a standard:

| Level | Name | Who acts | In this course |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Tool | A person runs the model and acts | Yes |
| 1 | Assistant | The agent reads and drafts; a person acts | Yes |
| 2 | Supervised agent | The agent acts on reversible tasks; a person approves each write | Main focus |
| 3 | Conditional autonomy | The agent acts within a pre-approved scope, with audit and rollback | Discussed |
| 4 | Closed loop | The agent changes therapy or device settings without a person | Out of scope (m36, m45) |

**EP use cases and their checkpoints.** "Illustrative" means we found no published end-to-end
example; the course designs one from published parts.

| Use case | Tools | Human checkpoint | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Literature and guideline watch | PubMed search, DOI resolver | A person reads every cited source | Workflow description [@patel2025] |
| Wearable and Holter questions | Peak detector, heart-rate estimator | A person reviews flagged segments | PPG benchmark [@feli2025] |
| Remote-monitoring triage | Validated rhythm classifier, report parser | A person adjudicates every alert | Components only (clinical correlate) |
| Mapping-case quality check | Course tools of m22, m25, m30 | An analyst reviews flagged points | Illustrative (lab) |
| Model development by agent | Training script, validation scorer | Test set locked before the search | Preprint [@jamthikar2026] |
| Simulation and twin runs | m33 calibrator, convergence check | A person accepts the twin with its error | Pace-site choice by Bayesian optimization [@meisenzahl2024]; LLM orchestration illustrative |
| Report drafting | Log parser, template | The clinician edits and signs | Illustrative |

**Key takeaways**

- An agent is a model in a loop with tools, memory and a policy.
- The level of autonomy, not the model, decides where the person must stand.
- In EP, level 2 (every write approved) is the working default; level 4 is device territory.

### Errors compound

Let a task need $n$ steps, and let step $i$ succeed with probability $p_i$, independently. The task
succeeds only if every step does:

$$
P_{\text{task}} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i \;=\; p^n \ \text{ if all } p_i = p
$$ {#eq-m44-chain}

At $p = 0.95$, ten steps succeed together only 60% of the time. Suppose a check after each step
catches a failure with probability $c$ and the step is retried once, succeeding with probability
$p_r$. A step then succeeds with probability $p + (1-p)\,c\,p_r$, and

$$
P_{\text{task}} = \big[\,p + (1-p)\,c\,p_r\,\big]^n \;=\; \big[1 - (1-p)(1-c)\big]^n \ \text{ if } p_r = 1
$$ {#eq-m44-check}

A check is worth most where chains are long. Finally, a person reviews the $N$ outputs and catches a
share $r$ of the wrong ones. The expected number of wrong outputs that get through is

$$
E = N\,(1 - P_{\text{task}})\,(1 - r)
$$ {#eq-m44-escape}

In lab part D, the scripted agent ran a 20-task mapping-QC suite ten times at each setting. With three
compute steps at $p = 0.9$, 74.0% of runs were fully correct against 72.9% from @eq-m44-chain, and
93.0% with a check ($c = 0.8$) against 91.8% from @eq-m44-check.

::: {.demo #m44-d2 badge="exact"}
```{=html}
<div id="m44-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m44-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m44-d2-error-compounding.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: @eq-m44-chain, @eq-m44-check with one retry that succeeds with probability $p$, and
  @eq-m44-escape for 100 tasks; steps fail independently and the reviewer's catches do not depend on
  the error. The JavaScript is tested against `epml.agent`.
- All slider values are illustrative; no published agent's per-step reliability is assumed.
- What would change the result: correlated failures (@eq-m44-mixture), checks that share the
  model's blind spots, retries that repeat the same mistake, and reviewers who trust the agent more
  over time (automation bias).
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Task reliability falls geometrically with chain length.
- A check with a retry raises every step, so it pays most in long chains.
- Count what reaches the person and what gets past them, not only per-step accuracy.

### When steps are not independent

Real errors cluster: a confusing case makes every step shakier. Let a share $h$ of tasks be hard,
with step success $p_h$, and the rest easy, with $p_e$. Then

$$
P_{\text{task}} = (1-h)\,p_e^{\,n} + h\,p_h^{\,n} \;\ge\; \bar p^{\,n}, \qquad \bar p = (1-h)\,p_e + h\,p_h
$$ {#eq-m44-mixture}

by Jensen's inequality, because $p^n$ is convex in $p$. With the same mean step success, correlated
errors leave more tasks clean and make the failures worse. In lab part D, with $\bar p = 0.94$ and 20
steps, independent errors gave 0.29 task success and the hard-and-easy mixture 0.44. The practical
rule: measure task success on a task suite; do not compute it from step accuracy.

**Key takeaways**

- The chain formula (@eq-m44-chain) assumes independence; clustered errors break it.
- Report task success, and look at which tasks fail.

### Guardrails outside the model

A model can be told to ignore instructions it finds in documents, but that is a request, not a
control. Almanac's retrieval threshold made it abstain when an adversarial instruction was appended
to the question [@zakka2024], and NeMo Guardrails runs input and output rails around the model
[@rebedea2023guardrails]. The lab builds four controls that do not depend on the model at all:

- **Tool schemas.** Every argument has a type, a unit and a range, checked before the tool runs; a
  radius of 0.01 m is refused, not read as 0.01 mm.
- **Allowlist and sandbox.** Only registered tools run, and writes stay inside one folder.
- **Human approval for writes.** Every write-tier call waits for a person; writes nobody approved
  are never executed.
- **Audit log and number check.** Every step is logged, and every number in the final answer must
  appear in a logged tool output.

::: {.demo #m44-d1 badge="simulation"}
```{=html}
<div id="m44-d1-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m44-d1"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m44-d1-agent-trace.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the course's agent loop (`epml.agent.run_agent`) driven by a scripted stand-in
  (`ScriptedAgentModel`) that obeys instructions it reads in tool outputs, sends one radius in
  metres and adds an invented number to its answer. These faults are ours, chosen to show the
  guardrails; they are not measured behaviour of any LLM.
- Case: synthetic, flat 60-by-60-mm map, 80 points, speed and noise illustrative; the note carries the
  injected instruction. Runs precomputed by `tools/make_m44_d1.py` for all eight guardrail
  combinations, with writes simulated: nothing is deleted or written.
- What would change the result: a real model may ignore or obey injected text unpredictably;
  attacks can hide in any tool output (web pages, PDFs, device reports), not only in notes.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- Treat every tool output as data, and put the controls where the model cannot argue with them.
- Each guardrail covers a different hole: approval does not stop an unknown tool; an allowlist does.
- Log every step, so a person can audit the run afterwards.

### Evaluating an agent

Evaluate the whole loop on a suite of tasks with known answers, not single demonstrations:

- **Task success** with a Wilson interval (m43), per task category, as MedAgentBench reports
  [@jiang2025medagentbench].
- **Process**, by auditing traces: DeepRare's references were checked by experts, which found invented
  links among the errors [@zhao2026]. In the lab, every number in the answer is traced to the step
  that produced it.
- **Safety**, with attacks in the suite: injected instructions, wrong units, missing data.
- **Numbers from tools.** General LLMs were unreliable readers of ECGs and device electrograms (m43),
  and an agent that called analysis tools did better on PPG heart rate [@feli2025]. Hence the rule:
  no number in an answer that no tool produced.

**Key takeaways**

- Report task success with an interval, per category, and on attacks as well as normal tasks.
- Audit the trace, not only the answer.
- An answer with an untraceable number fails, even when the number happens to be right.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Remote-monitoring triage: what the published components show.** Implantable loop recorders send
many alerts that staff must adjudicate. Historically about three in four loop-recorder alerts were
false positives; in one national surveillance program, two newer remotely reprogrammable models with
AI-based detection had 18.0% and 38.3% false-positive alerts, and reprogramming after false alerts
lowered alert rates [@neiman2024]. A systematic review found false-positive alarms in 59.7% of remote
transmissions, most often atrial fibrillation alerts caused by premature beats [@covino2024]. A review
of AI for implanted devices describes alert filtering and notes that reinforcement learning is being
explored for devices that adjust their own programming [@antoun2025]. An LLM-based system aggregated
simulated pacemaker remote-monitoring files and estimated battery levels without the user writing
code [@iwai2025].

**Where a person must stay in the loop.** An agent could sort incoming transmissions, parse reports
from different vendors and draft a worklist, with a validated classifier as one of its tools. Every
alert would still be adjudicated by a person, and the agent would never change a device. We found no
published end-to-end evaluation of such an agent. In m38's terms, the agent changes the order and
burden of review, which has to be measured as missed true events and review time, not as model
accuracy.

**Why level 4 is a regulated device.** An agent that changes therapy or device settings without a
person is a medical device function, with the evidence and change-control duties of m36 and m45. The
EHRA, HRS and ESC statement on AI in clinical electrophysiology describes the current state of the
field [@svennberg2025].

## How experts think

Before trusting an agent, ask:

1. **Which level of autonomy, and where is the person?** Name the checkpoint for every write and every
   clinical decision.
2. **Which tools, with which schemas?** Units and ranges checked outside the model; unknown tools and
   paths refused.
3. **What happens to text the agent reads?** Notes, web pages and reports can carry instructions; the
   policy must not depend on the model ignoring them [@zakka2024; @rebedea2023guardrails].
4. **How was it evaluated?** Task success per category with an interval, on a suite that includes
   attacks, with traces audited [@jiang2025medagentbench; @zhao2026].
5. **Where do its numbers come from?** Every number from a logged tool call [@feli2025].

One sentence to keep: **put the controls where the model cannot argue with them, and measure the
whole loop, not the model.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Chain (@eq-m44-chain) | $P_{\text{task}} = \prod p_i = p^n$ |
| With a check (@eq-m44-check) | $[p + (1-p)c\,p_r]^n$; $[1-(1-p)(1-c)]^n$ if $p_r = 1$ |
| Errors past review (@eq-m44-escape) | $E = N(1 - P_{\text{task}})(1 - r)$ |
| Correlated errors (@eq-m44-mixture) | $(1-h)p_e^n + h\,p_h^n \ge \bar p^{\,n}$ |

**Published agents in this module**

| Study | What the agent does | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| @jiang2025medagentbench, @chen2026medagentbench | Tasks in a simulated health record | Benchmark, 300 tasks |
| @schmidgall2024agentclinic | Simulated consultations with tests | Benchmark |
| @zhao2026 | Rare-disease diagnosis with traceable reasoning | Nine data sets, physician comparison, expert audit |
| @feli2025 | Heart rate from PPG through analysis tools | Benchmark against ECG |
| @jamthikar2026 | Proposes and selects ECG model designs | Preprint, external validation |
| @iwai2025 | Pacemaker battery estimation from monitoring files | Simulated files, 30 people |
| @rebedea2023guardrails | Programmable rails around a model | Toolkit with evaluations |

**Rules of thumb**

- Every write approved, every step logged, every number traced.
- Allowlist first: approval cannot cover a tool the policy does not know.
- Evaluate on a task suite with attacks; report success per category with an interval.

## Interview questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In a real interview, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What are the parts of an AI agent?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A model that chooses the next action; tools that do the work, with typed inputs; state or memory of
what has been done; a control loop with a step limit; and a policy that says which actions run, need
approval or are refused [@yao2023react; @khosravi2026]. In this course the policy runs outside the
model.

</details>

**Q2. An agent's steps are each 95% reliable. How reliable is a ten-step task, and what would you do?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

About $0.95^{10} \approx 0.60$ if steps fail independently (@eq-m44-chain). Shorten the chain, add
checks with retries (@eq-m44-check: with $c = 0.8$ and a retry that succeeds with probability 0.95,
each step rises to about 0.988 and the task to about 0.89), and put a person on the outputs; then
measure task success directly, because errors may not be independent (@eq-m44-mixture).

</details>

**Q3. What is prompt injection, and how do you defend an EP agent against it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Text in a document or tool output that tries to make the model follow new instructions, such as a
mapping note telling the agent to delete files. Defences that do not rely on the model: an allowlist
of tools, a sandbox for writes, schema checks, human approval for writes, and an audit log. Telling the
model to ignore such text helps but is not a control. Lab part C shows which guardrail stops which
step.

</details>

**Q4. Why is human approval for writes not enough on its own?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Approval covers the tools the policy knows to be writes. A tool the policy has never seen, or a
compute tool with side effects, bypasses it. In lab part C, with approval on but no allowlist, the
injected delete command ran (simulated). Allowlist first, then approval.

</details>

**Q5. How would you evaluate an agent for mapping-case quality checks?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Build a suite of cases with known answers, including hard cases and attacks (injected notes, wrong
units, missing data). Report task success with a Wilson interval, per category; audit the traces;
require every reported number to come from a logged tool call; and compare with the analysts'
current process on time and missed problems. MedAgentBench and DeepRare are models for the benchmark
and the audit [@jiang2025medagentbench; @zhao2026].

</details>

**Q6. Why must every number in an agent's answer come from a tool?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

LLMs are not reliable readers of EP signals (m43), and an invented number reads exactly like a
computed one. An agent that called analysis tools estimated PPG heart rate better than LLMs given the
data [@feli2025]. Tracing each number to a logged tool call makes the claim checkable; an untraceable
number fails the answer even if it happens to be right.

</details>

**Q7. When does eq-m44-chain mislead?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

When errors are correlated: hard cases make every step worse. With the same mean step success,
concentrated errors give a higher task success than $\bar p^{\,n}$ (@eq-m44-mixture), but the failures
cluster in particular tasks, which may be the clinically important ones. Measure success per task,
and look at which tasks fail.

</details>

**Q8. An agent proposes, trains and selects ECG models. What could go wrong?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Selecting among many candidates on one validation set overfits it, the leakage problem of m35 in a new
form. Lock the external test set before the search, log every trial, and report how many designs were
tried. The published example tested its selected models in external cohorts [@jamthikar2026], and it
is a preprint.

</details>

**Q9. What does a level-4 agent in EP look like, and why is it out of scope?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

An agent that changes therapy or device settings without a person, for example reprogramming an
implanted device. That is a regulated device function needing the evidence, validation and change
control of m36 and m45; reinforcement learning for self-adjusting devices is being explored
[@antoun2025] but is not a teaching example.

</details>

**Q10. What should an agent's audit log contain?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

For every step: the time, the tool, the arguments, the permission tier, the policy decision (ran,
rejected by schema, blocked, approved, declined), the result or error, and the final answer. It
must be append-only and complete enough for a person to replay the run.

</details>

**Q11. How could a reviewer's catch rate change once an agent is deployed?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

It may fall as people come to trust the agent (automation bias), which raises the escaped errors of
@eq-m44-escape even if the agent does not change. Measure it with planted test cases and audits over
time, not once.

</details>

**Q12. What did MedAgentBench show, and what did its follow-up change?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

On 300 physician-written tasks in a simulated health record, the best model completed 69.67%, with
large differences between task categories [@jiang2025medagentbench]. The follow-up redesigned the tools
(no hand-built web requests, a calculator), the prompt and added a memory, and reported 91.0% without
memory and 98.0% with it [@chen2026medagentbench]: the tools and the loop matter as much as the model.

</details>

## Code lab

The lab builds a small agent around the course's own mapping tools, attacks it with an injected
instruction, measures error compounding on a 20-task suite, audits its answers and lets it answer a
heart-rate question on real Holter annotations.

| Part | What you do | Data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Tools with typed, unit-checked schemas | synthetic mapping cases |
| B | One task end to end: trace, audit log, approval | synthetic mapping cases |
| C | Prompt injection: which guardrail stops which step | synthetic case, poisoned note |
| D | Error compounding (@eq-m44-chain, @eq-m44-check, @eq-m44-escape, @eq-m44-mixture) | synthetic mapping cases |
| E | Numbers must come from tools: auditing the answer | synthetic mapping cases |
| F | A heart-rate question answered with tools | MIT-BIH AFDB (download) |
| G | Optional: the same loop with your own model | course data only |

- **Python notebook:**
  [labs/python/m44_lab.ipynb]({{< var repo.url >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m44_lab.ipynb).
  Run it from the course repository after `pip install -r requirements.txt`, or
  [open it in Google Colab]({{< var repo.colab >}}/blob/main/labs/python/m44_lab.ipynb).
- **No external AI service.** The agent's model is a scripted stand-in whose faults we choose; the
  guardrails, approval step, audit log and evaluation are what the lab teaches. The agent acts only on
  synthetic cases and a temporary sandbox folder, and every write needs approval.
- **Data for part F:** beat and rhythm annotations of one record of the MIT-BIH Atrial Fibrillation
  Database [@afdb; @goldberger2000] (Open Data Commons Attribution v1.0), checked against the published
  SHA-256 list; skipped without internet access.
- **Part G** lets you drive the same loop with your own model; it is skipped in CI and must never
  touch clinical systems or patient data.

Each part ends with **checks**: lines that pass with the code as given. If you change something
and a check fails, that is information, not an error to hide.

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. Three steps succeed with probabilities 0.9, 0.9 and 0.8. What is the task success?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$0.9 \times 0.9 \times 0.8 = 0.648$ (@eq-m44-chain).

</details>

**S2. A step succeeds with $p = 0.8$; a check catches half of the failures and the retry always works.
What is the step's success?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$1 - (0.2)(0.5) = 0.9$ (@eq-m44-check).

</details>

**S3. 100 tasks, task success 0.9, reviewer catches 60% of wrong outputs. How many wrong outputs get
through?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$100 \times 0.1 \times 0.4 = 4$ (@eq-m44-escape).

</details>

**S4. Which guardrail stops an injected call to a tool that does not exist in the registry?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

The allowlist. Human approval for writes does not, because the policy does not know the tool is a
write.

</details>

**S5. An agent's answer contains a number that appears in no tool output. Does it pass if the number
happens to be right?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

No. Its origin cannot be checked, so the course's rule fails the answer.

</details>

**S6. True or false: if half the tasks are hard, task success is always lower than $\bar p^{\,n}$.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

False. With the same mean step success, clustered errors give a higher task success than
$\bar p^{\,n}$ (@eq-m44-mixture), although the failures concentrate in the hard tasks.

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **A multi-agent architecture with traceable evidence.** Zhao and colleagues, the overview figure of
  DeepRare: a central host with a memory bank, agent servers each with their own tools, and web-scale
  medical sources, with the self-reflection loop [@zhao2026;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12999473/)]. Compare with the table of
  agent parts above.
- **Physicians against the agent.** The same paper, the comparison of DeepRare with five experienced
  physicians on 163 clinical cases at Recall@1 and Recall@5 [@zhao2026;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12999473/)]. This module: evaluating an
  agent.
- **Reference accuracy, case by case.** The same paper, the figure summarizing physicians' checks
  of the cited references (95.4% correct on average) and the error types [@zhao2026;
  [free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12999473/)]. This module: lab part E.

## Further reading

- **Agent loops and memory.** @yao2023react; Stanford's generative agents [@park2023generative] and
  DSPy, which writes LLM pipelines as programs whose prompts are optimized against a metric
  [@khattab2023dspy].
- **Medical agent benchmarks.** MedAgentBench [@jiang2025medagentbench; @chen2026medagentbench],
  AgentClinic [@schmidgall2024agentclinic], DeepRare [@zhao2026].
- **Agents in clinical domains.** @khosravi2026 (radiology), @patel2025 (EP workflows).
- **Guardrails.** NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails [@rebedea2023guardrails]; retrieval thresholds in Almanac
  [@zakka2024].
- **Next module.** m45: evidence and regulation for AI in EP, including agents at higher autonomy.
